title: Aramco Reveals 2.6 Billion Barrel Loss From Hormuz Crisis; Russia Seaborne Exports Collapse 33%; Syria Offers to Drop Russian Oil Under US Sanctions Pressure
subhead: Aramco quantifies the war toll at 2.6 billion barrels lost globally and warns inventories need 18 months to refill, while Russian seaborne product exports fell a third in July after Ukrainian drone strikes on refineries, and Damascus pledges to slash Russian crude imports in exchange for US sanctions relief.

sections.heading: Aramco Quantifies the Damage: 2.6 Billion Barrels Lost, 18 Months to Rebuild
sections.body:
Saudi Aramco CEO Amin Nasser said the US-Iran war has removed more than 2.6 billion barrels of oil from global markets since February — equivalent to nearly a month of normal world crude production. Speaking alongside the company's Q2 results, which showed a 44% jump in net profit to $32.69 billion, Nasser said that even if the Strait of Hormuz reopened today, it would take up to 18 months at 2.1 million bpd to replenish depleted inventories (Reuters/Zawya).

Aramco's total hydrocarbon production averaged 9.5 million bpd in Q2, down from 12.8 million bpd a year earlier, as the company rerouted shipments away from Hormuz through its East-West Pipeline. Nasser said recent attacks on Aramco facilities caused some production interruptions but had no material financial or operational impact. He warned that strong refining margins globally signal continued tightness in product markets, with refineries running near maximum capacity and few buffers to absorb further outages (The News Pakistan, Zawya).
sections.whyItMatters: Aramco's 2.6 billion barrel figure is the first comprehensive corporate estimate of cumulative supply loss from the Hormuz closure — it puts a number on what markets have only guessed at, and the 18-month replenishment timeline suggests the supply shock will persist well beyond any diplomatic resolution.

sections.heading: Syria Offers to Slash Russian Oil Imports in US Sanctions Bargain
sections.body:
Syria has told the United States it is willing to drastically reduce imports of Russian oil — currently around 60,000 bpd, up 75% this year — as part of discussions over lifting the State Sponsors of Terrorism designation that has been in place since 1979. Three sources familiar with the talks told Reuters that Damascus committed to the reduction, though the US did not explicitly frame it as a precondition for delisting (Reuters, US News, Kyiv Post).

A Syrian source said Damascus relies on Russian crude out of necessity, not preference: 'Lift the SST designation and we will buy oil from somewhere else.' Syria has already signed a gas deal with ConocoPhillips and Novaterra in June and is discussing offshore exploration with TotalEnergies. Separately, Georgia's only refinery confirmed it is phasing out Russian oil under EU sanctions, shifting to Kazakh and Libyan supplies (Kyiv Post).

Congress has directed the Pentagon to assess options for reducing Russia's military presence in Syria, including its Tartous naval base and Hmeimim airbase. Trump notified Congress on July 8 of his intent to remove Syria from the SST list, triggering a 45-day certification window (US News, Reuters).
sections.whyItMatters: Syria's pivot away from Russian oil — in exchange for sanctions relief — is a concrete illustration of how the US is weaponizing economic access to squeeze Moscow's remaining client states. If implemented, it would end Russia's position as Syria's dominant crude supplier and open Syrian energy to Western firms.

sections.heading: Russian Seaborne Oil Product Exports Plunge 33% After Ukrainian Strikes
sections.body:
Russia's seaborne oil product exports fell by a third in July to about 3.9 million metric tons, according to Reuters-cited data from industry sources, reflecting a sharp drop in fuel production after Ukrainian drone attacks on Russian refineries. Russian crude processing hit its lowest level since May 2002 at an estimated 3.6 million bpd — roughly one-third below the seasonal average of 5.3-5.6 million bpd (Bloomberg via Moscow Times, Oilprice).

Ukraine struck 18 refineries in July, surpassing the previous monthly record, and expanded its campaign to tankers, pipelines, and export infrastructure. Only four tankers loaded crude at Novorossiysk in the week ending July 26, down from seven to eight in prior weeks. Russia has extended its diesel and gasoline export bans through 2027 to secure domestic supply, and domestic fuel shortages have pushed Russian companies to seek imports from India, Belarus, and Kazakhstan (Reuters, Kyiv Post, Oilprice).
sections.whyItMatters: The 33% drop in seaborne product exports is the clearest quantitative evidence yet that Ukraine's drone campaign is achieving what sanctions alone could not: a meaningful reduction in Russian fuel output and export capacity. The extension of export bans signals Moscow cannot meet both domestic and export demand simultaneously.

sections.heading: Oil Steadies Near $79 as Hormuz Deal Optimism Clashes With Operational Reality
sections.body:
Brent crude steadied around $79 per barrel on August 5, after dropping more than 5% on Tuesday on optimism about a Hormuz transit deal. WTI traded near $75. The selloff followed Qatari and Pakistani mediators saying they had reached 'very progressive stages' in drafting an interim proposal for the strait, and US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent saying a deal could come 'today or tomorrow' (CNBC TV18, The Guardian, FXStreet).

But tanker traffic at Hormuz remains at a two-month low, with the VLCC Egypt Prosperity aborting a transit attempt over the weekend after direct radio threats and nearby explosions. Kpler analyst Matthew Wright told the BBC the security situation is 'the worst period since this crisis began.' Iran is discussing a temporary transit scheme with Oman that would route ships along a corridor near Iranian waters, with tolls deferred to a 60-day negotiating period — but Oman is reportedly resisting, fearing the arrangement could become permanent (Oilprice, The Guardian).

Goldman Sachs said it expects Brent to trade in an $80-$90 range until either a confirmed US-Iran deal or a major escalation, with the potential to reach $120 if three simultaneous chokepoint crises deepen (Reuters, 247 Wall St).
sections.whyItMatters: The gap between diplomatic rhetoric and on-the-water reality is widening. Markets are pricing in a deal, but tanker operators are not risking transits — and the proposed Oman corridor leaves Iran with enduring leverage over Gulf shipping even under a temporary arrangement.

sections.heading: Big Oil's War Windfall: BP and Marathon Post Record Profits as Refining Margins Soar
sections.body:
BP reported Q2 profit of $5.73 billion, more than doubling from $2.35 billion a year earlier, driven by higher oil and gas prices and refining margins amplified by the Hormuz disruption. BP raised its dividend by 4% and projected 2026 capex of $14 billion. The results drew criticism from campaigners accusing the company of profiteering from the conflict (Reuters, MSN, Yahoo Finance).

Marathon Petroleum posted a four-fold profit increase to $5.14 billion in Q2, its highest quarterly profit since 2022, as refining margins doubled on supply disruption. Devon Energy reported $1.9 billion in Q2 net earnings, its best quarter since 2022, following its merger with Coterra that boosted production to the upper end of forecasts (Reuters, Seeking Alpha, Oilprice).

Reuters described it as a 'refining golden era' in an analysis piece, but warned the boom will not last — margins are a function of temporary supply disruption, not structural demand growth. Aramco's Nasser echoed this, noting the industry has few buffers for further outages (Reuters, Oilprice).
sections.whyItMatters: The war is transferring wealth from consumers to producers and refiners at a staggering pace. The political backlash — Trump has publicly blasted Big Oil for 'making too much money' — makes windfall taxes or price controls more likely the longer the conflict drags on.

sections.heading: US Critical Minerals Push Stumbles: Pentagon Cancels $300M Lithium Tender, Lockheed Signs Scandium Deal
sections.body:
The Defense Logistics Agency canceled a $300 million lithium carbonate tender for the national defense stockpile on August 3, after twice extending the bid deadline. The solicitation had sought nearly 36 million pounds (16,000 tons) of battery-grade lithium carbonate over five years. The cancellation follows a similar failed $500 million cobalt tender last year, signaling persistent difficulties in procuring critical minerals at fixed prices for multi-year contracts (Oilprice, Bloomberg, MSN).

In contrast, Lockheed Martin signed an MOU with NioCorp for up to 15 metric tons per year of scandium oxide over 10 years, building on an existing Skunk Works joint development program. Lockheed is also negotiating germanium supply deals with 5N Plus and Teck Resources, all part of a Pentagon-driven push to cut dependence on Chinese critical minerals (Seeking Alpha, Reuters, MSN).

Separately, Energy Fuels began construction on a commercial-scale heavy rare earth expansion at its White Mesa Mill in Utah, backed by a $725 million conditional government loan. The project will produce terbium and dysprosium by end of 2027, with further expansions planned through 2029 (Forbes).
sections.whyItMatters: The Pentagon's lithium failure exposes the core problem in US mineral strategy: the government can identify strategic needs but cannot execute multi-year procurement contracts in volatile markets. The scandium deal shows that targeted, smaller-scale agreements with domestic producers are more achievable than large stockpile purchases.

sections.heading: India Diversifies Away From Gulf: HPCL Buys Nigerian Crude, ONGC Builds 13M-Barrel Storage
sections.body:
Indian refiner HPCL bought 2 million barrels of Nigerian crude (Okwuibome and Utapate grades) from Glencore via tender for its Rajasthan refinery, as term supplies from the Middle East remain trapped west of the Strait of Hormuz. HPCL's managing director Vikas Kaushal said the company 'hardly got anything from our term contracts' in Q1 because cargoes were stuck in the Persian Gulf (Reuters, Oilprice).

India's imports of Russian crude hit a record high in July, accounting for more than half of total imports. Indian refiners are also testing crude from Angola and Venezuela to offset lost Middle Eastern supply (Oilprice, Economic Times).

Meanwhile, ONGC will build a 13-million-barrel storage facility in Mangaluru, with half reserved for strategic reserves and half for commercial operations. India's current maximum reserve capacity covers only eight days of national oil demand — among the lowest of any major importer. The estimated investment is $1.6 billion (Oilprice, The Print India).
sections.whyItMatters: India's structural vulnerability — eight days of reserves versus the IEA's 90-day standard — is forcing rapid diversification and storage investment. The shift toward Russian, Nigerian, and Venezuelan crude is reshaping trade flows that may persist even after Hormuz reopens.

bottomLine: Aramco's 2.6 billion barrel loss figure and 18-month replenishment estimate put a hard number on the cumulative supply shock from the Hormuz closure, even as oil prices dip on deal optimism that tanker operators are not yet acting on. The diverging signals — diplomatic progress on paper, worsening security on the water — define the current moment. Meanwhile, Ukraine's drone campaign has cut Russian refining to a 24-year low and seaborne product exports by a third, Syria is bargaining away Russian oil access for US sanctions relief, and India is spending billions to fix an eight-day reserve buffer that the war has exposed as dangerously thin. The refining windfall for BP, Marathon, and Devon is politically volatile: Trump is already attacking oil companies for profiting from a crisis his administration is struggling to resolve.
sources: Reuters, Zawya, The News Pakistan, US News, Kyiv Post, Bloomberg, CNBC TV18, The Guardian, FXStreet, Oilprice, Forbes, Seeking Alpha, MSN, Yahoo Finance, BBC, Moscow Times, CNBC, 247 Wall St, Anadolu Agency, UNI India, The Print India, Economic Times
